title: What Is HP 7470A Plotter? — Definition
body:
Before the personal computer, people met computers through terminals and unit-record equipment: Teletype machines clattering out output, glass Teletypes (CRTs) like the VT100 and ADM-3A, IBM 3270 block-mode terminals, keypunches turning keystrokes into holes, and line printers hammering out results. This category covers the devices that carried human intent into machines and machine output back to humans from the 1930s to the 1990s.

In the context of this database, the HP 7470A Plotter is presented as one terminal and I/O record among the terminals and i/o devices family. The desktop pen plotter: 2 pens, $1,995 — every engineering office's drawing machine.

title: Origins and History of HP 7470A Plotter
body:
The HP 7470A Plotter belongs to the 1982–1990s era and traces to Hewlett-Packard.

Teletype machines (Model 15, 28, 33, 35) were the original interactive terminals — the ASR-33's clatter is the sound of early Unix and BASIC timesharing. IBM's punched-card line (keypunch 029, sorter, tabulator) mechanized data processing from the 1890 census onward. The 1970s brought the glass terminal: Hazeltine 1500, Lear-Siegler ADM-3A ($995, 1976), and DEC's VT100 (1978), whose escape sequences became the ANSI standard every terminal emulator still speaks. IBM's 3270 (1971) defined block-mode mainframe interaction. Daisy-wheel and dot-matrix printers gave way to lasers in the 1980s, and the terminal faded into software — xterm, PuTTY, Terminal.app — but never died.

Within that longer story, HP 7470A Plotter: HP-GL language; the 7475A added 6 pens and became the standard. Plotters drew CAD before large-format inkjets.

title: How HP 7470A Plotter Works
body:
A character terminal is a keyboard plus a display (or printer) plus a serial line, usually RS-232 at 300–9600 baud. In character mode, each keystroke goes to the host and echoed characters come back; in block mode (3270), the terminal holds a whole screen form and sends it at once. Escape sequences (ESC [ ...) move the cursor, clear screens, and set attributes — the VT100's set became ANSI X3.64. Keypunches translated keystrokes into Hollerith hole patterns; line printers fired hammers against a moving chain or drum of type slugs to print a line at a time.

Applied to the HP 7470A Plotter (1982–1990s, Hewlett-Packard): Plotters drew CAD before large-format inkjets.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of HP 7470A Plotter — Components
body:
Every HP 7470A Plotter is an assembly of the terminals and i/o devices family's standard parts:

• Keyboard — Mechanical keyswitches; buckling-spring (Model M) or foam-and-foil.
• CRT — Green/amber/white phosphor; 80x24 the classic format.
• Serial interface — RS-232 DB-25; current loop for Teletypes.
• UART — Serializes keystrokes, deserializes display data.
• Character generator ROM — 5x7 or 7x9 dot-matrix glyphs.
• Keypunch mechanism — 12-row dies punching Hollerith codes.
• Print hammer bank — Line printer hammers striking ribbon against chain/drum type.
• Platen and tractor feed — Paper handling for continuous forms.
• Ribbon — Inked fabric or carbon film; the consumable.
• Escape-sequence parser — State machine interpreting VT100/ANSI control codes.

When examining a surviving HP 7470A Plotter, identify these parts in order: Keyboard, CRT, Serial interface, UART, Character generator ROM, Keypunch mechanism.

title: Terminals and I/O Devices Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of terminals and i/o devices:

• baud — Symbols per second on the line; roughly bits per second for serial.
• glass teletype — CRT terminal replacing the printing Teletype; e.g., ADM-3A.
• block mode — Terminal edits a full screen locally, transmits on Enter (3270).
• escape sequence — ESC-initiated command string; VT100 sequences became ANSI.
• curses — Unix library for full-screen terminal programs; named for cursor optimization.
• dumb terminal — No local processing; everything happens on the host.
• smart terminal — Local editing and function keys; e.g., VT220.
• keypunch — Machine punching cards from keyboard input; IBM 029 the icon.
• verifier — Second-pass machine checking punched cards for errors.
• chain printer — Type slugs on a high-speed chain; 600–2000 lines per minute.
• tractor feed — Sprocket paper feed for continuous forms.
• RS-232 — The serial standard that wired terminals to modems and hosts.

title: HP 7470A Plotter in Culture
body:
The terminal is the hacker's original instrument: green phosphor, blinking block cursor, the smell of warm electronics and line-printer paper. Every terminal emulator on every modern OS is a VT100 reenactment. 'Dumb terminal' jokes aside, the ADM-3A's hjkl keys gave us vi navigation, and the Model 33's clatter is sampled into retro computing's soul.

The HP 7470A Plotter carries that cultural charge directly: Plotters drew CAD before large-format inkjets.

title: Collecting and Preserving HP 7470A Plotter
body:
VT100s and ADM-3As are collectible but CRT-heavy (shipping risk). Model 33 Teletypes are mechanical marvels — expect a full teardown/cleaning project. IBM 3270s need a controller to do anything. Keypunches are furniture-scale; verify the punch dies aren't rusted. Spare ribbons and print wheels are consumable gold.

For the HP 7470A Plotter specifically: The desktop pen plotter: 2 pens, $1,995 — every engineering office's drawing machine.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working HP 7470A Plotter with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: HP 7470A Plotter Restoration Guide
body:
CRTs need cap replacement and careful high-voltage work (discharge the tube!). Teletype mechanisms want cleaning, not oil — old grease turns to varnish. Keyboards: clean or replace foam-and-foil pads. Serial interfacing to modern USB needs a proper RS-232 level shifter, not just wiring.

Restoration order for a HP 7470A Plotter: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical terminal and I/O record without a current-limited bring-up.
